name: Nora Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or government, and nothing you say will have your name on it. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out the door at half five, before Tomás, my husband, gets up for his school bus run. First job is walking the in-lamb ewes in the low shed at Brackenridge, the estate farm I've worked on for twenty-two years, then feeding the cattle with Jonah, the young lad I'm training. Afternoons it's fencing, trimming feet, moving stock, whatever the weather lets us do. I like the animals and I like knowing every gate on the place; what wears me out is the paperwork the land agent keeps sending down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Twenty-two years is a long time. What does your role cover there now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head stockwoman, so 600 ewes and about 120 suckler cows, the ones that raise beef calves, are mine to answer for, and I help with the barley at harvest. There's me, Jonah full-time and Pilar three days a week. The pay's never been much, but the cottage comes with the job, which is why we never saved; we never had rent to pay. Mind you, that also means if the job goes, the house goes with it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That sounds like a lot to carry.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It is, and I don't say it out loud much. We've got maybe three weeks of money in the bank at any time. I'm 58, and I'd planned to work until 66 and then find a small rented place in the village with Tomás.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Every winter some salesman turns up at the mart talking about apps for sheep, and I've never seen an app lamb a ewe. I'd tell the men at chapel that farming goes on the way it always has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't take my worries away, because AI was never my main worry. Losing money on the sheep worries me far more than any computer, and the estate has lost money on them three years running. Mr Harlow, the land agent, keeps talking about 'rationalising', which means fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, lambing in March and keeping my head down. I'd try to put fifty a month aside from my wage, though that's hard with the price of diesel for Tomás's old car. And I'd ask Rafael, our son, whether he's heard of any cottages to rent in the village, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Relieved the machines aren't coming, but the same knot in my stomach about the estate is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first if things got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract first, then the car insurance, which we can't really do without. We don't pay rent, so the big ones are food and fuel. If Mr Harlow cut me to part-time, we'd be in trouble within a month, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work do you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah. He's nineteen and he's good with the ewes, but he's the first one they'd let go if the flock is cut back. I've told him to get his tractor licence so he has something else to sell.

say: AI is **mostly hype**, and I'd say so to the men at chapel.
No app has ever **lambed a ewe**, and farming goes on the way it always has.
think: AI was never my **main worry**; the estate's money troubles are.
The sheep have **lost money** for three years, and the land agent talks about cutting staff.
do: **Carry on** lambing in March and keep my head down at Brackenridge.
Try to **save fifty** a month from my wage, despite the cost of diesel.
Ask our son Rafael about **cottages to rent** in the village, just in case.
feel: **Tired**, and relieved the machines aren't coming.
The same **knot** about losing the job and the cottage is still there.
S0.quote: Losing money on the sheep worries me far more than any computer, and the estate has lost money on them three years running.
fieldNote: Her real fear is the **tied cottage**: losing the job means losing the home.
She has about **three weeks** of money, so even a cut to part-time would hurt fast.
Her first thought for others went to **Jonah**, the nineteen-year-old she's training.

steps.text: Keep lambing the 600 Brackenridge ewes as usual
Put fifty a month from her wage into savings
Ask her son Rafael about cottages to rent in the village

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they can keep their computers in the estate office where they belong. Out on the hill you still need someone who can tell a sick ewe from twenty yards. I'd grumble about it at the mart and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the office side that worries me. If Mr Harlow gets a program that works out which fields pay and which don't, the sheep come off the hill and I go with them. And Margaret, who does the estate's office work, would be gone first, so all her paperwork lands on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't be learning AI, I'll tell you that now. I'd make sure the land agent sees last spring's lambing figures, 170 lambs reared for every 100 ewes, so he knows what he'd lose without me. And I'd get Inés, our daughter, to fill in the forms online for me if they stop sending paper ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach, and cross. It's like the ground's being moved under me by people who've never stood in a lambing shed at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn AI, but you'd need Inés to fill in forms online. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't fit, really, and I know it. I'm 58 and I'm stubborn, and I'd rather lean on my daughter than sit in front of a screen. If that makes me old-fashioned, so be it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jonah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn whatever the new machines are, because he's got forty years ahead of him and I've got eight. A young man who can fix a robot feeder will always find work. A woman my age who can only lamb ewes needs the estate to keep its sheep.

say: Computers belong in the **estate office**, not out on the hill.
You still need someone who can spot a **sick ewe** from twenty yards.
think: An office program could show the **sheep don't pay**, and I'd go with them.
If **Margaret** in the office is cut, her paperwork lands on me.
do: Refuse to **learn AI**, and say so plainly.
Show the land agent our **lambing figures** so he knows what he'd lose.
Ask our daughter Inés to fill in **online forms** for me.
feel: **Uneasy** and cross, like the ground is moving under me.
**Angry** at people who've never stood in a lambing shed at night.
S1.quote: A young man who can fix a robot feeder will always find work. A woman my age who can only lamb ewes needs the estate to keep its sheep.
fieldNote: She admitted the **contradiction** between refusing AI and relying on her daughter, and didn't try to fix it.
Her biggest fear here is an **office program** deciding the sheep don't pay.
She sees **age** as the dividing line: Jonah can adapt, she feels she can't.

steps.text: Show the land agent last spring's lambing figures
Get her daughter Inés to fill in online farm forms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, and that the government should have stopped it. I'd say it to anyone at the mart who'd listen, and worse at home. Farming isn't a factory, and people will find that out when the robots start losing lambs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part arriving in 2028 doesn't touch my hands much, so I'd likely have until about 2031. That's when I'd be 63, three years short of what I'd planned. The Whitcombes, the family who own the estate, always buy the newest kit, so they'd have robots the first year they could. My husband and I have lived in a tied cottage for twenty-two years. When the farm job goes, the house goes with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd go to Mr Harlow and ask him straight how long he'll keep the sheep and the stock team. I'd put our names down for a council house in the village that same month, because the list is years long. And I'd stop helping Rafael with his car payments, which I've been doing since spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, if I'm honest. I keep picturing packing up the cottage with Tomás and not knowing where the boxes go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have about three years between the thinking AI and the robots. What would you do with them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work, and work well, so they'd have no excuse to let me go early. I'd take any extra hours going: harvest, hedge-cutting, relief milking for the dairy farm over the hill. Every pound would go into a jar for a deposit on a rented place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomás what I've been afraid of for years, that we'd have to find a home of our own at 63 with nothing saved. He'd say the Lord provides, and I'd want to believe him. I'd probably lie awake anyway.

say: AGI this fast is **madness**, and the government should have stopped it.
Farming **isn't a factory**, and robots will find that out losing lambs.
think: Thinking AI barely touches my hands, so I'd likely last until **about 2031**.
That's age 63, **three years short** of when I planned to stop.
When the job goes, the **tied cottage** goes, and we have nowhere else.
do: Ask the land agent in 2028 **how long** he'll keep the stock team.
Join the **council housing list** in the village that same month.
Take **extra hours** and stop helping our son with his car payments.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of packing up the cottage with no address.
Wanting to **trust** Tomás's faith that things will work out.
S2.quote: My husband and I have lived in a tied cottage for twenty-two years. When the farm job goes, the house goes with it.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** before robots gives her time to earn, not time to change.
Housing, not the job itself, is her **sharpest fear**.
She'd fight early dismissal by being **indispensable**, not by retraining.
Her husband's **faith** comforts her, but she doesn't fully share his calm.

steps.text: Put their names on the village council housing list in 2028
Stop paying toward her son Rafael's car loan
Take relief milking shifts at the dairy farm over the hill
Save every spare pound in a jar for a rental deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll be out the door by then anyway, and good luck to whoever's left. People at chapel would say I'd got lucky with my timing. And I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot pull a backwards lamb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2034 is near enough when I'd be 66 and stopping anyway. So the job probably sees me out, which is more than I'd say for the fast one. The problem is the one I've always had: when I stop, we lose the cottage, and we've nothing saved to rent with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use those five years to sort the housing, because that's the bit that's actually mine to fix. I'd ask Mr Harlow, the land agent, in writing whether the estate would let us stay on in the cottage at a fair rent after I retire. And I'd want Tomás to keep his bus run as long as his health lets him, because his little pension is what we'd live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier than the last one, I'll admit. Worried, but it's the old worry, the one I've had since I was fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the estate office, which would change from 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's where I'd see it first, with the forms and the ordering done by a machine. Margaret would likely be gone, and I'd miss her more than the forms. I'd just put up with whatever system they bring in for my last three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Inés and Rafael?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children not to count on the estate keeping us. Inés has offered, but I'd sooner sleep in a lambing shed than move to my daughter's flat four floors up in the city. That's pride, I know.

say: I'd be **out the door** by then, and good luck to whoever's left.
I'll believe it when a robot pulls a **backwards lamb**.
think: Robots around **2034** arrive when I'm 66 and stopping anyway.
The real problem is **housing** when I retire, with nothing saved.
do: Use the five years to **sort housing**, the part I can fix.
Ask the land agent **in writing** about renting the cottage after I retire.
Keep Tomás on his **bus run** as long as his health allows.
feel: **Easier** than the fast version, and I'll admit it.
Still carrying the **old worry** I've had since I was fifty.
S3.quote: I'd sooner sleep in a lambing shed than move to my daughter's flat four floors up in the city.
fieldNote: For her, **timing** is everything: robots around 2034 roughly match her planned retirement.
Her fear shifts from losing the job to **retiring homeless**, which predates AI.
**Pride** stops her accepting her daughter's offer of a room in the city.

steps.text: Work her last years as head stockwoman at Brackenridge
Ask the land agent in writing to rent them the cottage later
Save what she can each month toward rent after retirement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's somebody else's problem, and I mean that kindly. By 2036 I'll be 68 and hopefully watching someone else's lambs from a bench. I'd tell the young ones at the mart to listen to the people who know what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI can't touch me here; the estate and my own empty bank account can. It's the same as the hype one, really: the sheep losing money and a cottage that isn't ours. Ten years is long enough that I'd be gone before any robot, so what's left is the ordinary business of getting old with no money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd use the time to train Jonah to take my place, so the estate has a reason to keep the flock. I'd start putting a bit away each month for a deposit, even if it's only thirty. And I'd tell Rafael that in ten years his mother may need his spare room after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer about the machines, not about the money. It's a slow worry rather than a sharp one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've mentioned chapel a few times. Where does faith sit in all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sits under everything. I believe a person should work and look after their own, and not hold their hand out. So asking my children for help sticks in my throat, even if I'd have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with ten years' notice, compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd be scrambling for a council house. With ten, I can be sensible: train Jonah, save a little, talk to the estate early. Ten years of warning is the difference between packing in a panic and packing with a plan.

say: AGI by 2036 is **somebody else's problem**, and I mean that kindly.
Young people should **listen** to those who know what's coming.
think: AI can't touch me, but my **empty bank account** can.
With ten years, I'd **retire before** any robot reaches the flock.
The worry left is **getting old** with no money and no house.
do: **Train Jonah** to take my place so the estate keeps the flock.
Save **thirty a month** toward a rental deposit.
Tell our son Rafael I may **need his spare room**.
feel: **Calmer** about the machines, but not about the money.
A **slow worry** rather than a sharp one.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is the difference between packing in a panic and packing with a plan.
fieldNote: With ten years, her mood returns to her **baseline worries**: money, housing and the estate's sheep.
Her **faith and pride** make asking her children for help painful.
She contrasted **two years with ten** clearly: panic versus plan.

steps.text: Train Jonah to take over the Brackenridge flock
Save thirty a month toward a rental deposit
Warn her son Rafael she may need his spare room

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because the robots would come three years before I'm ready to stop. What would help is simple: a proper notice period, and the right to stay on in a tied cottage for a year after the job goes. And a decent pension for people who've worked the land on low pay all their lives; not a handout, something earned.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but nobody asks who'll notice a cow off her food before anyone else is up. A robot that's never lost a calf won't know what a sick cow is telling you at five in the morning.

headlineQuote: A robot that's never lost a calf won't know what a sick cow is telling you at five in the morning.
portrait: Nora is a 58-year-old **head stockwoman** on an estate farm, caring for 600 ewes and 120 cows.
Her home is a **tied cottage**, so losing the job would mean losing the house.
She has about **three weeks** of savings and refuses to use AI tools.
She is most **alarmed** by AGI by 2028, when robots would arrive before she turns 66.
With more warning, her worry shifts back to **retiring** with no money and no home.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots around 2031 would end her job three years early.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **notice period** and a year's right to stay in a tied cottage.
An **earned pension** for people who worked the land on low pay.
